messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard error (the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean under H₀) is  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.22 .
\]
message.reasoning:
The user says "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" but they provide sample mean, sample std dev, sample size, and population mean. They likely want the standard error or something? Actually they say "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". That might refer to the standard error of the sampling distribution under H0: sqrt(σ^2/n). But we don't know population sigma; we have sample std dev as estimate. So standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40)=6.3249. 1.4/6.3249=0.2215 approx. So answer ~0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For t-test, t-statistic uses sample std dev. Standard deviation of t distribution depends on df. But they ask "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". Might be standard error. I'll give that.

Thus output: 0.2215.
